newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo civil servants get first pay in months.
newsitem.headline: Congo civil servants get first pay in months.

text.p: An army of neglected civil servants got their first pay packet in months on Thursday but found Laurent Kabila's effort to restore order in his new Congo unimpressive.

"In other countries people are happy with pay day but here it is a day of sadness," post office employee Pelenge Samba said as he picked up a month's salary -- a wad of notes enough to make him a millionaire in New Zaires but worth only around $20.
If Kabila, the new president who ousted veteran leader Mobutu Sese Seko last month, had hoped for gratitude he will be disappointed. Numerous disgruntled workers complained as they took their money.
"This money won't help for nothing -- it's like being given just a tip," grumbled another postal worker Victor Boa.
Hundreds of an estimated 600,000 state employees queued up at banks in the centre of the capital Kinshasa to collect the pay, originally announced for Wednesday but delayed a day.
Kabila's government said it would pay one month's salary to employees, but no back pay -- at least for now -- and no wage rise because the country is bankrupt.
"Nothing has changed yet. They are still using the pay scale left by Mobutu. So what's new?" said Boa.
Finance Minister Mawapanga Mwana Nanga said the money -- a total bill of up to some $20 million -- would be found from meagre government revenues.
He says no more "New Zaires" will be printed. They are now worth about 110,000 to the dollar but will be replaced by the Congolese franc later this year.

In a worrying sign for Kabila, soldiers from his own army, angered by their own pay dispute, fired off rounds for up to half an hour in the jungle city of Kisangani in the east on Tuesday, residents and local church radio reported.
They started firing in the crumbling city centre after some were paid in dollars, others in local "Zaire" currency and some not at all, residents said.
Civil servants, who earn between one and four million New Zaires a month, are some of the worst paid people in a country where an estimated 70 percent have no job at all.
"It's an insignificant salary but we have no choice. With $18 I can't make ends meet," said Jean-Marie Dambota of the foreign ministry.

Most workers like him gave up relying on Mobutu's crumbling state and put their real efforts into second jobs to scrape a living. Many rely on hand-outs or even their wives' prostitution to earn the money to raise a family.
Mawapanga says civil servants will have to start to work properly and those who do not will be laid off en masse as part of efforts to restore order to a sector full of "fictitious workers".
Decades of economic indiscipline ruined what could have been one of Africa's richest states.
Mobutu is said to have stashed away billions of dollars and to have enriched his followers at the expense of the population.
